pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: How does a key like "alice" end up in a specific bucket? And what three properties make a hash function good for table use?
expected_points: the hash function turns the key's bytes into a fixed-size integer
the bucket index is hash mod the number of buckets
good means deterministic, uniformly spread, and fast — not cryptographic

questions.prompt: Two different keys land in the same bucket. Compare how separate chaining and open addressing each handle this, and name one advantage of each.
expected_points: chaining keeps a linked list per bucket and walks it
open addressing probes other slots in the same array (e.g. linear probing)
chaining tolerates high load and has easy deletion; open addressing is cache-friendly with no per-entry pointers
collisions are inevitable (pigeonhole) — the strategy is part of the table's definition

questions.prompt: What is the load factor, why does your table resize when it passes 0.75, and what does the resize actually cost?
expected_points: load factor = entries / buckets; chains lengthen as it grows
resizing doubles the buckets and re-inserts (rehashes) every entry because index = hash mod bucket count changes
a single resize is O(n), but doubling makes it amortized O(1) per insert — same argument as slice append

questions.prompt: Walk me through what your Put does, step by step, when called with a key whose bucket already holds two other entries.
expected_points: hash the key and fold it into a bucket index
walk the chain comparing keys; replace the value in place on a match
no match: check the load factor (resize if needed), then link a new entry into the chain and grow size

questions.prompt: Hash tables are advertised as O(1) but their worst case is O(n). Explain both claims and what pushes a real table toward the worst case.
expected_points: average: uniform hash + bounded load factor keeps chains at a small constant length
worst: all keys in one bucket degenerates into a linked-list scan
drivers: a bad hash function, never resizing, or adversarial keys crafted to collide (hash flooding)

questions.prompt: Deleting from your chaining table was just unlinking a node. Why is deletion trickier in open addressing?
expected_points: lookups follow the probe sequence until the key or an empty slot
emptying a slot punches a hole that ends other keys' probe sequences early
so deletions leave a tombstone marker meaning keep probing

questions.prompt: Connect this lesson to the Go map you have used since S1: what are comma-ok and delete under the hood, and why is iteration order randomized?
expected_points: the built-in map is a hash table; comma-ok is Get, the delete builtin is Delete
bucket order is a meaningless artifact of hashing, so Go randomizes iteration to stop code depending on it
a per-process random hash seed also makes crafted-collision attacks harder
